Hi Eric, hi listfolk,

This took a wee bit of digging...

P3 is there because it has exactly the same form as the R3 formula that
was already implemented (so it was easy when we implemented point
transects). As you say, it also handles the important case in which the
number of visits to each point is different. We haven't got around to
implementing all of the estimators yet (though this is on my current
todo list).

Do you know that encounter rate varies over the study area? You could
compute the encounter rate and if that leads you to conclude large
variation in encounter rate then perhaps a geographical (or temporal)
post-stratification scheme might help?

Hope this helps!

cheers,
--dave

Hello,

I'm relatively new to both distance sampling and R and am running in to some issues with my analysis of Antarctic Prion burrows on Macquarie Island:
I can't get the code for fitting a ddf in the worked example Multiple covariate detection function (MCDS) analysis of crabeater seals <http://distancesampling.org/R/vignettes/crabeater-mcds-2014.html> (.Rmd <http://distancesampling.org/R/vignettes/crabeater-mcds-2014.rmd>, data <http://distancesampling.org/R/vignettes/crabbieMCDS.csv>) working. It keeps returning the following error: Error in `contrasts<-`(`*tmp*`, value = contr.funs[1 + isOF[nn]]) : contrasts can be applied only to factors with 2 or more levels. R tells me that the variable I am trying to query is a factor with 2 levels, so I'm not sure what is going on.
When trying to fully stratify my data following the example Stratified study region for minke whales in the Southern Ocean <http://distancesampling.org/R/vignettes/minke.html> (.Rmd <http://distancesampling.org/R/vignettes/minke.Rmd>, data <http://distancesampling.org/R/vignettes/minke.csv>) I run into an issue that 2 of 8 strata have too few detections to fit detection functions. This means when I come to add up all the AIC values to compare with AIC values for models using stratum as a covariate and of pooled data I'm effectively missing two values. Basically the results seem incomparable so I for the remainder of the analysis I've gone with the model using stratum as a covariate.
When I come to try to generate density and abundance estimates for each stratum something weird is going on. In the table generated the total Effort comes out as 262 (presumably km) but only 157 km of transect were completed.
In the abundance estimate generated one stratum was barely sampled because it was essentially unsuitable cliff habitat. But in the short area sampled 3 detections were made. This results in a massively high density estimate for the stratum and a huge and inaccurate overall contribution to the overall population estimate.
It strikes me as odd that nowhere does the analysis appear to require information on transects along which no burrows were detected. This is obviously very important when estimating overall density/abundance within a stratum.
Sorry for such a long list. I've attached my data, R code, and an additional file with all transect info which includes those transects along which no burrows were detected.

If I can figure all of this out I'd like to move on to applying density surface models to my data. Thanks for a great set of R packages.

Jez

messages.body_plain:
Nick,

I didn’t look over your code, but if you did the distance sampling correctly you will obtain an estimate of the number of pellets on the landscape. If you can make some assumptions about how long they last on the landscape and defecation rate of the deer, you can simply adjust the pellet estimate accordingly.

For example, if you estimates 250 pellets/ha and deer defecate at 1.5 times per day over the 30 days they could exist on the landscape then 250/(1.5*30) is the deer density. If you have estimates of the defecation rate then you could incorporate that error into your density estimate using the delta method. I think this is what Marques et al. did in their paper  https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1046/j.1365-2664.2001.00584.x

You should be able to  incorporate those defecation rates (with SE) into Distance as an adjustment factor and it will do the hard work for you.

Regards,

Duane

Loading required package: mrds

5) Your data *should* include information on transects without detections.  The lack of detections is important information for the analysis. messages.body_plain:
Jez

I've spent a bit of time with your data, and I need your help to understand your survey design and data organisation.

> head(prions)
  Study.area Region.Label     Area Sample.Label     Effort distance size slope veg_height observer
1       2515            5 16.64778            1 0.03361597      0.3    1     D          S       PP
2       2515            5 16.64778            2 0.03361597      0.5    1     D          S       PP

Conventionally, the first field, Study.area, represents the name of the study area, hence there is customarily a single value for all records.  I don't know the rationale for different values for study.area.

For region.label, you have 8 unique values, which makes sense.  Half of the strata have <35 detections (strata 1, 4, 5, and 7)

I presume the units in which region area is specified is km^2 (because the total of the 8 stratum areas is roughly the size of the island).

Sample.Label confuses me, because the

> length(unique(prions$Sample.Label))
[1] 2605

This is two orders of magnitude larger than the number of transects we are accustomed to seeing in a survey.  And the lengths of the transects (units km?) are also surprisingly small 33m?  You noted in your email you were hoping eventually to construct density surface models; have you specified segmented transects as the samples here?

Distance is, hopefully, the perpendicular distance to the burrows.  However, the units of measure for perpendicular distance is not consistent with the units of measure for region area and transect length.  That is why the covered area in the model output vastly exceeds the size of the island.  Best to convert distance units to km as well.  Out of curiosity, how large in diameter are the burrows?  I note your measurements are to the nearest 10cm(?).  Is this the distance to the burrow entrance centre?  That would be best.

I have nothing to say about your item 3) where you suggest total effort in the data does not match your belief that 157km were surveyed.  Nor do I have comments regarding transects without detections.  As I noted earlier, all survey effort needs to be recorded in the data, even effort that did not result in detections.

Think of the data organisation of a line transect survey in a hierarchical fashion:

A single study area divided (perhaps) into strata.  Within each stratum, there are transects.  On (most/some) transects there are detections.  This will permit estimation of density/abundance from a design-based perspective.  If preparing to use density surface models, transects are subdivided into segments; but the hierarchy remains in that under that situation, detections belong to segments.

Once we are on the same page, then we can make progress.

I am preparing a project to assess feasibility of UAVs for surveying guanacos, a large ungulate that has social structure (forms family and juveniles groups).

The plan is to use strip transects as a way to survey the populations. Then we will compare p´citures at regular intervals and video.

As part of the assessment I would like to simulate different strip widths.

The issue is then how the strip widths may affect the estimation for animals living in groups. Then, it may be the case when the strip of pictures or video captures part of a group.

It can be assumed that the animals out of the strip  (and of sight)  may be balanced with animals from another group inside the band. But I wonder if something can be done for get a more precise sstimation.

I would like to make simulations with DSsim, but as far as I understand, DSsim simulates groups of individuals as "points" with a group size as an attribute , and not as individuals clustered in the space.

An option would be to build a population object out of DSsim and then bring it as the population object to be surveyed in DSSim, but I don´t know if this is possible.

Any ideas or workaround are welcome.

messages.body_plain:
Andre

The subject of using mass of each species as a covariate in the distance sampling detection function was mentioned on the list a couple of weeks ago.  The answer to your question "can I use this" is "yes"; making mass a continuous covariate.  You can also use species name as a factor, rather than continuous, covariate in the detection function.  The question of which approach to use depends upon the number of species you are including, and whether the change in detectability is a smooth function of mass, or perhaps a discontinuous function of species behaviour.

The simplest example of how to implement this would be to use the Distance software, including species as a factor covariate, you can then post-stratify on your species covariate.  Then request density estimates at both the global and stratum layer and detection function at the stratum layer.

This become less straightforward in the presence of additional covariates; and I'm not certain how this would be carried out in the Distance software.  I'm also do not know how this would be done in the Distance R package.  Perhaps others could shed light upon these alternative analyses.

Jez

Happy to read you have found your missing effort.  I worry that effort not accounted for by analysts who ignore transects without detections is more common that acknowledged.  Here are a variety of comments based on your last email.

To your model fitting problem:

You cannot use the function ddf() because ddf() expects fields in your data (object, detected) that you do not have.  The function ds() in the Distance package circumvents this problem.

Regarding the problems with model fitting: there are still problems with your data file, for many observations, the observer covariate is missing, causing complaints from the ds() function.  Examining your csv file with a text editor reveals

The other thing to know about ds() and ddf() is they were designed with "double observer" surveys in mind.  Hence the field name "observer" carried special meaning for these functions.  Renaming the final field in your data something other than "observer" resolves the error you were having.

names(prions)[10] <- "whom"

prion.observer <- ds(prions, truncation=prion.trunc,
                      key="hn",  formula=~whom)

Use of multiple covariates and modelling philosophy

Distance sampling, unlike mark-recapture, has the property of model robustness, meaning that unbiased estimates are still obtained even if not all sources of variability in detection are incorporated. Hence, it is not common to fit an exhaustive candidate model set to data.  We have lectures and exercises on the use of covariates in detection function modelling found at

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter5/

There you can find discussion of modelling strategies with covariates and examples of such analyses

Designs for stratum-specific abundance estimates

The approach you have taken with your design, to cut across habitat types with continuous transects, and essentially post-stratify after data collection is a bit awkward.  If your objective was to produce stratum-specific estimates, then allocating effort within the strata of interest would have been a safer route.  Note this discussion on our list back in 2014 about a design similar to yours:

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/distance-sampling/tiago%7Csort:date/distance-sampling/owhsicU2888/vspY9W6fJF8J

Also note that your data seem to tell you that birds hardly use 4 of your habitat types.  Your inference about burrow density in the strata with <50 detections produce CVs > 0.30, hence pretty wide confidence intervals.  Contribution of strata 1, 4, 6 and 7 to the overall abundance estimate is ~5%.

Mattia/Group

Mattia privately shared his Distance project with me so I could run my fingers through the data to find to source of the error message.  The solution turned out to be simple, but the message that Distance generated in the Log window was deceptive.

There were indeed 5 segments in the data with an effort (length) of 0.  The problem was trying to find them.  There is a check box in Analysis | Preferences that lets you see the data as Distance begins processing it.  By checking that box (below) I could have a look at the segment-level data:

Notice the print statement at the top of the window.  Distance is printing the contents of an R data frame.  The 32nd row of that data frame contains a record with 0 Effort; one of the segments Distance was complaining about.  However, the offending segment is not the segment carrying the label 32; but instead the 32nd record in the data frame.  The data frame uses a mangled variant of the segment labels (e.g. "1. 1" and "1026. 1026") and sorts the data frame on the basis of that character representation of the segment label.

By trolling through this echo of the data, we can find that there is effort of 0 associated with segments labelled 551, 1026 (the one shown above), 2139, 2397 and 3030.  Those should be repaired and the data re-imported.

That explains the nature of the error message, but it exposes a more general issue associated with segmenting line transect data.  These 5 segments with 0 associated effort were always the last segment in a transect.  If you look through the data further, you will find, in addition to the 5 segments with 0 effort, there are 9 segments with effort (lengths) of 1m.  Segmenting of transect data by cutting transects into equal lengths with the remainder falling into the last segment can lead to arithmetic challenges of "no leftover" in some segments, and perhaps worse, very small segments always at the end of transects.  Should detections arise in those small segments, they can have a disproportional influence on the density surface modelling.

messages.body_plain:
Good morning Scott.

I'm guessing about the cause of the warning you have received.  It might be caused by a stratified analysis; in which you are requesting density by stratum and using mean cluster size for each stratum.  There may be one or more strata where all recorded clusters were of size one.

Unrelated to your specific question, by relevant to your study of orchids on host trees; have a look at the section in Chapter 8 of the Users Guide that may be of relevance:

Zero Cluster Sizes in CDS Analysis
There are some situations where you may observe clusters of size zero. For example, imagine that you are surveying for a species of parasitic plant that only occurs in a certain tree. You survey by walking a line transect looking for trees, and if you find one you approach it and count the parasitic plants in the tree. One way to enter these data would be by recording the distance to each tree, and the number of parasitic plants in each tree as the cluster size. You may find no plants in a tree, in which case you record a cluster size of zero.

This section goes on, but perhaps this introductory paragraph grabs your attention.

messages.body_plain:
Nicole

Not sure about your specific question.  Observations regarding your output:
lots of detections >4000; must be combining all species, correct?  Are species likely to share a common detection function?
use of survey date in the model is a bit of a blunt instrument; you will see that the SEs are as large as many of the daily coefficient estimates.  Is there an abiotic factor, e.g., wind/rain that might be a better mechanistic predictor of change in detectability between days; leading to a more parsimonious model?
Lack of model fit - based upon the CvM test using exact distances as well as the chii-square analysis; this is partially a consequence of your large sample size; but also considerable rounding to favoured distances (5, 10, 15, 20,...)
not very good precision at the stratum level; coefficients of variation are roughly 100%; meaning the standard error of the density estimate is roughly equal to the estimate itself.  This makes inference weak.
unusual study design with but a single point in each site (based on what I seen in the results).  With that design, there is no way to estimate encounter rate variance (variability in detections between points within a stratum).  This source of variation is usually responsible for roughly half of the uncertainty in point transect density estimates.  This means your density estimates likely have even more uncertainty that the results indicate.
Let me know if I am off-base with my assessments.  Any matters you want to further discuss?

Hi Anthony, hi listfolk,

Quick reply to these:

1. it's not possible to get vis.gam to talk to ggmap as they use
different plotting systems. Instead you need to make predictions over
some grid of the space/other covariates then plot that using ggplot's
geom_tile, you can then add in a ggmap. Two important things here: 1.
(perhaps obviously) you need to turn down the opacity on the geom_tile
layer to see the background, 2. the prediction grid needs to have all
your covariates in it, note that vis.gam will take averages for the
covariates not displayed (median for continuous, mode for factors), so
the plot you currently have may not be accurate depending on your model
(see the cond argument to vis.gam for more information).

2. Regarding the plots, the Q-Q plot doesn't look great, you're right.
You could try using the negative binomial distribution (nb() in mgcv).
Resids. vs linear predictor plot is not interpretable in this form as
for count data it's hard to see any patterns in the deviance residuals,
use rqgam.check to get a better version using randomised quantile
residuals (and see the reference therein for how to interpret). A full
explanation of the gam.check output is available in Simon Wood's GAM book.

cheers,
--dave

Nicole

If distance sampling concepts are giving your difficulty, may I recommend that you take our online distance sampling workshop:

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/
That will provide you with grounding on the principles.  I suggest you pay particular attention to Chapter 3 that deals with point transects, such as you have undertaken.  Once you have mastered the basics, you can then visit Chapter 7, that describes carrying out these analyses in R.  Specifically for dealing with multi-species surveys such as yours:

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter7/#multi-species-survey---montrave-line-transects
Specifics of your data:

I've done a small examination of your data.  I encourage you to restrict your enthusiasm for lots of detection modelling; there is much to learn before you get to that point.  You should begin with a statement of what you want to learn.  What are your objectives?  Do you wish to make comparisons between sites, between species, between seasons?  Not clear from what you've disclosed thus far.

I suggest some preliminary analyses, looking at what your data show.

nicole <- read.csv("2017.2018 Distance.csv")
names(nicole)
with(nicole, table(Site, Observer))
options(max.print = 99999999)
with(nicole, table(Species, Site))

>From this you can see there is confounding between observer and site; some observers only visited some sites; that will make including both site and observer in detection function modelling problematic.  You can also see from the second table there are data entry errors for "goldfinch" and "crow".   Note too that there are few species detected on all sites and for a number of species, across all sites there will be too few detections to fit defensible detection functions.  You may need to make decisions about grouping species into guilds that may share similar detectabilities.

To conduct species-specific analyses, see the code below (and more elegant code in the online exercise I mention above)

library(Distance)
amro <- ds(data=nicole[nicole$Species=="American Robin",],
           truncation=75, key="hn", transect="point")
plot(amro, pdf=TRUE)
amro.fit <- gof_ds(amro)

I truncate to a distance where the detections are mostly noise and ask for a plots showing the probability density function.  You will see that the model fails to fit, due to pronounced spikes in the data caused by rounding to favoured numbers.
Perhaps these hints will enable you to make progress.

Eric Rexstad

I failed to mention, if you are recording the information about each visit separately (by including the date), then your effort field should not represent the total number of visits, but rather a single visit.  Alternatively, if you remove visit-level covariates and pool detections across visits, then effort would be recorded as total number of visits.

>
> I've done a small examination of your data.  I encourage you to restrict your enthusiasm for lots of detection modelling; there is much to learn before you get to that point.  You should begin with a statement of what you want to learn.  What are your objectives?  Do you wish to make comparisons between sites, between species, between seasons?  Not clear from what you've disclosed thus far.
>
> I suggest some preliminary analyses, looking at what your data show.
>
> nicole <- read.csv("2017.2018 Distance.csv")
> names(nicole)
> with(nicole, table(Site, Observer))
> options(max.print = 99999999)
> with(nicole, table(Species, Site))
>
> From this you can see there is confounding between observer and site; some observers only visited some sites; that will make including both site and observer in detection function modelling problematic.  You can also see from the second table there are data entry errors for "goldfinch" and "crow".   Note too that there are few species detected on all sites and for a number of species, across all sites there will be too few detections to fit defensible detection functions.  You may need to make decisions about grouping species into guilds that may share similar detectabilities.
>
> To conduct species-specific analyses, see the code below (and more elegant code in the online exercise I mention above)
>
> library(Distance)
> amro <- ds(data=nicole[nicole$Species=="American Robin",],
>            truncation=75, key="hn", transect="point")
> plot(amro, pdf=TRUE)
> amro.fit <- gof_ds(amro)
>
> I truncate to a distance where the detections are mostly noise and ask for a plots showing the probability density function.  You will see that the model fails to fit, due to pronounced spikes in the data caused by rounding to favoured numbers.

> Perhaps these hints will enable you to make progress.

Domingos

"Monotonicity" means a function going in the same direction (always increasing or staying the same; or decreasing and staying the same).  Distance sampling operates on the premise that a detection function will be at its highest on the transect, and will decrease (or remain the same) at increasing distances.

When fitting a detection function to your data, the software finds that the best fit to your data would be for the detection function to increase, because at some distances from the transect, you are detecting more piles of dung.  As a consequence, the software is issuing a warning (rather than an error) stating that the software wants to do two things that are in conflict.  Namely, the software is trying to produce the best fit of the function to your data while at the same time trying not to allow the detection function to increase with increasing distance from the transect.

The warning message is informing you that the software has made the decision to produce a function that does not increase at the expense of a function that passes through some heightened number of detections  in your data.

Hope this is helpful.

Domingos

A warning (orange) message means that you should examine the results of the programme carefully because, in this case, something unexpected occurred.  Unexpected does not mean an error took place.

As described in my earlier message, the monotonicity constraint warning would be interpreted as there is an increase in detections at some distance off the transect.  Distance has not allowed the fitted detection function to have a "bump" causing the detection to rise, so as to better fit that increase in detections.

The question to ask your self is "do I believe that rise in detections at distance is real, or is it a result of noise in the data (is it caused by process or stochasticity).  In almost all cases, the bump is a result of noise in the data, it which case, the detection function should not be fitted to noise, but rather to process.  In which case, the warning can be ignored because Distance has "done the right thing" by not fitting to the noise in the data.

Nevertheless, it is important to go thought this decision process when a warning is encountered.

Eric Rexstad

messages.body_plain:
Nicole

Several issues here:

Covered area:  you cannot explicitly specify it.  It incorporates the number of times the point is visited; so it is covered area * number of visits.  Note also that covered area is measured in the same units that distances were measured in (metres?) while Area is measured in whatever units you used; the ds() function does not check for consistency in measurement units; that's the users' responsibility.
Truncation distance:  model selection tools (AIC) are not useful in determining truncation distance.  It is a subjective decision based upon an assessment of the distance beyond which detections are not providing useful information about the decay of the detection process (the process you are trying to model with the detection function.
Sense checks of P_a estimates: while your estimates of P_a might be sensible (0.10-0.22)--you must be the judge of whether there are 5-10 birds for each one you detected.  Note however, that for your model with lowest AIC (observer as covariate), the SE(P_a) is enormous--sometime >1.0  That must be wrong.  If you dig into your results for models with observer as covariate, you will see the parameter estimates for these models are non-identifiable.  Specifically the coefficient associated with Observer "R" and Observer "J" have SEs that are really large.  I suspect those two observers had too few detections to do a good job of estimating the nature of their detection function.
